content: 1. Uterine tone increases in a dose-dependent manner, but a single dose does not enhance uterine tone at term gestation (Oats, 1979). 2. Animal studies suggest that ketamine use does not reduce uterine perfusion, as it increases uterine blood flow (Levinson, 1973; Craft, 1983; Strümper, 2004; Tsen, 2009). 3. Ketamine has positive effects on maternal hemodynamics, but its side effects, such as delirium and hallucinations, have limited its routine use for cesarean sections (Bovill, 1971). 4. Etomidate induces anesthesia rapidly with minimal cardiovascular effects. 5. Intravenous administration of etomidate can cause pain and involuntary movements during recovery. 6. Etomidate is associated with nausea, vomiting, potential seizure activation, and impaired glucocorticoid response to stress (Bergen, 1997). 7. Although etomidate crosses the placenta immediately, the umbilical-vein-to-maternal-vein ratio varies significantly (0.04 to 0.5) (Gregory, 1991; Esener, 1992). 8. Etomidate at 0.3 mg/kg is associated with better neonatal acid-base balance compared to thiopental at 3.5 mg/kg (Downing, 1979). 9. A transient reduction in neonatal cortisol production has been observed when etomidate is used for general anesthesia induction (Crozier, 1993). 10. Midazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine, has minimal adverse cardiovascular effects and provides hypnosis and amnesia during anesthesia maintenance (Kuczkowski, 2007). 11. Midazolam crosses the placenta rapidly, with an umbilical-vein-to-maternal-vein ratio of 0.66 (Bach, 1989). 12. No significant differences in maternal hemodynamics have been reported between midazolam and thiopental (Crawford, 1989; Celleno, 1993). 13. Some studies suggest midazolam is associated with a higher incidence of low Apgar scores and neurobehavioral impairment in neonates compared to thiopental (Bland, 1987; Ravlo, 1989; Celleno, 1993). 14. Due to unclear clinical benefits, midazolam is recommended as a hypnotic for cesarean sections only when other induction agents are unsuitable (Tsen, 2009). 15. Benzodiazepines, particularly midazolam, have amnestic effects, and some anesthesiologists administer them after delivery to prevent anesthesia awareness (Robins, 2009; Lesage, 2014). 16. Opioids, commonly used as painkillers and during general anesthesia induction in non-obstetric patients, are avoided in cesarean sections due to concerns about neonatal respiratory depression (Lesage, 2014). 17. Short-acting opioids, such as fentanyl, alfentanil, and remifentanil, are used to stabilize hemodynamic changes during and after endotracheal intubation, especially in women with pre-eclampsia, hypertensive disorders, cerebral aneurysms, or heart disease (Maghsoudloo, 2011; Allen, 1991; Ashton, 1991; Yoo, 2013; Booth, 2011). 18. Adequate uterine contractions are crucial for preventing postpartum hemorrhage (WHO, 2008). 19. Volatile halogenated anesthetic agents inhibit uterine contractions in a dose-dependent manner and may cause anesthesia-induced uterine atony, but they are still widely used for general anesthesia maintenance during cesarean delivery (Turner, 2002; Yoo, 2006; Peach, 2009; Murdoch, 2013). 20. General anesthesia for cesarean sections is associated with increased blood loss compared to regional anesthesia (Heesen, 2013; Butwick, 2014). 21. Volatile anesthetics may inhibit uterine contractions, contributing to increased blood loss (Butwick, 2014). 22. The incidence of blood transfusion is not higher with general anesthesia compared to regional anesthesia (Heesen, 2013). 23. Using intravenous anesthetics instead of volatile agents for general anesthesia maintenance may reduce postpartum hemorrhage and uterotonic dosage. 24. Excessive uterotonic administration can lead to multiple organ failure, particularly heart failure, and other fatal maternal events (Henriques, 2007). 25. Replacing volatile halogenated anesthetics with intravenous anesthetics may improve maternal mortality and morbidity. 26. Hypnotic drugs used in general anesthesia can affect the fetus via uteroplacental transfer, potentially causing neonatal depression (Tsen, 2009). 27. Neonatal depression is multifactorial, involving maternal, placental, fetal, and external factors (Mattingly, 2003). 28. Preterm neonates are more susceptible to anesthetic-induced depression than term neonates (Laudenbach, 2009). 29. Urgent cesarean sections increase maternal complications (Pallasmaa, 2008; Ghazi, 2012). 30. Most hypnotics reduce vascular tone, leading to hypotension after general anesthesia induction (Tsen, 2009). 31. Maternal hypotension can impair uteroplacental perfusion, reducing placental blood flow (Hoyt, 2012). 32. A decrease in maternal systolic blood pressure increases the incidence of fetal bradycardia (Ebner, 1960). 33. Although maternal hypotension is transient, it may cause fetal acidaemia (Corke, 1982). 34. Minimizing fetal depression and ensuring maternal hemodynamic stability are critical in managing general anesthesia for cesarean sections. 35. Sodium thiopental, a short-acting barbiturate, has been the most commonly used hypnotic agent for cesarean sections for over half a century (Murdoch, 2013). 36. The safety and efficacy of thiopental for general anesthesia induction in term and preterm cesarean sections have been confirmed (Ong, 1989). 37. Thiopental rapidly crosses the placenta, but fetal brain concentrations rarely exceed the threshold for neonatal depression, allowing the neonate to be awake at delivery while the mother remains unconscious (Tsen, 2009). 38. The mean umbilical-artery-to-umbilical-vein ratio of thiopental is 0.87, with an induction-to-delivery interval of 8 to 22 minutes (Morgan, 1981). 39. Thiopental concentrations in the umbilical vein do not reach levels used for general anesthesia in adults and are typically around 4 mg/kg (Kosaka, 1969). 40. Factors contributing to a sleeping mother and an awake baby include active transfer of thiopental to the fetal liver, difficulty increasing fetal brain concentrations due to the water-rich fetal brain, rapid redistribution of thiopental from fetus to mother, heterogeneity of intervillous blood flow, and dilution of thiopental in fetal circulation (Farragher, 2003). 41. Propofol, a rapid-onset and short-acting hypnotic agent, is the most frequently used intravenous anesthetic for non-obstetric patients and has been included in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines since 2011 (WHO, 2013). 42. Due to the unavailability of thiopental in some regions, propofol has gained popularity in obstetric anesthesia (Murdoch, 2013; Rucklidge, 2013).
